title: Skim+Annotate: sparse attention, chunked caches, and pragmatic eval heuristics (scratchpad)
content:
Goal: very rough, personal reading synth for sparse attention + cache strategies that could be realistic to test on Redwood Dedicated/private nodes. Mostly a memory of my reading + small sketches for experiments.

High-level takeaways (sketchy):
- Sparse attention (block/sparse patterns) can greatly reduce runtime for long contexts but often requires careful batching and kernel support. Not magic: tradeoffs in information flow across distant tokens.
- Chunked KV caches (per-segment compressed summaries + exact recent KV) feel promising for user-facing apps where most latency is at generation time; we can keep exact KV for last N tokens and compressed/indexed summaries for earlier segments.
- Eviction policy matters: purely recency-based eviction is simple but loses thematic continuity across long sessions. Heuristics that keep topic anchors (named entities, slot fillers) give better perceived coherence.
- Evaluations: standard perplexity/ROUGE not sufficient. Need small human-proxy metrics (slot retention, fact recall over turns) and cheap automated probes (is-entity-still-known, prompt-cloze tests).

Paper skims and notes (very compressed):
- 2004.05150 (BigBird / sparse random + block + global)
  * Strength: provable approximation to full attention, graph-based connectivity.
  * Prod relevance: randomness + block structure might be implementable on top of existing kernel planner; but we need assess GPU memory patterns — some patterns break continuous memory access.
  * TODO: check memory strides on A100 vs GH200 for block + random sampling; note between-samples batching impact.

- 2004.08761 (Longformer-style sliding window + global tokens)
  * Very pragmatic for sliding-window tasks (long docs). Global tokens for question/summary anchors are interesting — could map to ‘system context’ + ‘user-query anchor’.
  * Danger: if global tokens become bottleneck for many parallel requests, routing + sharding becomes necessary.

- 2301.00808 (FlashAttention and kernel-level speedups)
  * Kernel engineering wins matter more than algorithmic sparsity alone. FlashAttention shows that rethinking memory layout + compute order reduces runtime dramatically.
  * For Redwood runtime: collaborate with serving-runtime team to see if sparse-block kernels (packed blocking) benefit from same layout changes.

Design / heuristics I keep returning to:
- Hybrid KV cache layout:
  * recent_exact: circular buffer of raw KV for last R tokens (R smallish, e.g., 2k tokens) — preserve exact retrieval and generation speed.
  * segment_summaries: for each preceding chunk (size C=4k-8k), keep a compressed representation: either low-dim projection of keys or a small dense vector per chunk that is expanded back into pseudo-KVs for coarse attention.
  * index_of_interest: small table of anchors (entities, intents) extracted from user messages; preserve these as persistent 'global' tokens in cache.

- Eviction heuristics (sketch):
  * score each chunk by recentness * importance. Importance approximated by: named-entity density, recency of mention in current turn, explicit user pin.
  * Evict the lowest scoring chunk; but periodically (every M evictions) run a cheap recall probe: sample a user QA that used older context and check retrieval score. If recall drops below threshold, try keeping that chunk longer.

Cheap eval probes to implement quickly:
- Anchor retention test: seed a small chat session containing 6 entities, then query about entity facts at intervals (after 1k, 5k, 10k tokens). Measure hit rate.
- Cloze continuity test: generate cloze prompts that depend on information that appeared N tokens earlier; success rate as function of N.
- Latency vs cost curve: measure tail latency while enabling chunk-summaries with varying decompress costs; look for knee point where latency increases but per-token GPU cost decreases.

Open questions / mental TODOs:
- How lossy can segment summaries be before downstream hallucinations spike? Quick experiment: compress to dim 64 vs 256 and see entity recall.
- Is it better to synthesize pseudo-KVs from summaries at request time or maintain cached pseudo-KVs (more storage, less compute)? Storage vs compute tradeoff depends on model size and disk/SSD cost.
- How to make eviction explainable to users (for enterprise)? Could surface list of pinned anchors and last-kept-chunk timestamps in Console.

Experiment sketches (short-term):
1) Minimal pilot on CPU/GPU VMs: implement segment_summaries = mean-pooled projection of keys (dim=128). Test on synthetic long-chat dataset (50k tokens) for anchor retention probe. Track recall + latency.
2) Ablation: vary R (recent exact) from 1k to 4k and C (chunk size) from 2k to 8k. Measure generation quality and GPU-time-per-token.
3) Heuristic eviction: implement importance score and compare to pure LRU over user sessions sampled from product logs (anonymized). Metric: fraction of sessions with semantic break (automated QA probes).

Implementation notes / infra considerations:
- Need serving-runtime hooks to: 1) fetch compressed chunk(s) quickly from SSD/disk or in-memory cache; 2) optionally expand pseudo-KVs in CUDA kernels. If expansion is on CPU-host, watch PCIe transfer overhead.
- Caching on Dedicated nodes: evaluate whether persistent SSD cache per-node (for private) vs in-RAM ephemeral cache gives better SLO tradeoffs.
- Telemetry: track which anchors are consulted per-request and their age. Add a low-overhead trace to Console to visualize cache hits over token index.

Notes-to-self / rough links to backlog: (very rough)
- Put pilot under branch: github.com/redwood-inference/kv-cache-experiments -> pilot/hybrid-summary-2028-11
- Slack thread: #kv-cache (ping Kai + Eliot) for quick sync.
- Add confluence page INFR-llm-cache-notes-2028 with findings and plots.

Quick heuristics for when to use which approach in product: (very opinionated)
- Short conversational assistants (<8k context): keep simple exact KV; avoid compression unless memory budget tight.
- Long-document summarization or analytics: prefer sparse-block attention + chunk summaries; allow slightly higher latency for better cost scaling.
- Multi-turn personalization (weeks-long state): persist anchors + select chunk caching for key user metadata; sync to object store for low-memory clients.

Action items (next 2 weeks):
- Build synthetic anchor retention probe harness (dataset + metrics) — assign: me.
- Prototype segment_summaries projection (dim=128) and basic expansion on CPU — assign: Kai.
- Get a short dev meeting with serving-runtime to discuss kernel-level options and memory layout (Eliot to coordinate).

Random thoughts / stray notes:
- Could borrow ideas from approximate nearest neighbor memstores: maintain per-chunk small ANN index to pick candidate chunks for expansion. Might be overkill initially.
- For enterprise users, easy-to-understand knobs (recent_exact_size, chunk_size, anchor_persistence_days) will be better than opaque ML-driven eviction.

End of scratchpad. Keep terse, iterate on pilot results, and move promising ablations to internal eval harness.
summary: Personal exploratory notes about sparse-attention and KV-cache strategies for long-context inference; includes paper skims, heuristics, experiment sketches, and short-term action items.
